According to Du Boulay, "Tutu's politics spring directly and inevitably from his Christianity."[457] He believed that it was the duty of Christians to oppose unjust laws,[141] and that there could be no separation between the religious and the political just as—according to Anglican theology—there is no separation between the spiritual realm (the Holy Ghost) and the material one (Jesus Christ).[458] However, he was adamant that he was not personally a politician.[457] He felt that religious leaders like himself should stay outside of party politics, citing the example of Abel Muzorewa in Zimbabwe, Makarios III in Cyprus, and Ruhollah Khomeini in Iran as examples in which such crossovers proved problematic.[459] He tried to avoid alignment with any particular political party; in the 1980s, for instance, he signed a plea urging anti-apartheid activists in the United States to support both the ANC and the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC).[460] Du Boulay, however, noted that Tutu was "most at home" with the UDF umbrella organisation,[461] and that his views on a multi-racial alliance against apartheid placed him closer to the approach of the ANC and UDF than the blacks-only approach favoured by the PAC and Black Consciousness groups like AZAPO.[462] When, in the late 1980s, there were suggestions that he should take political office, he rejected the idea.[463]

When pressed to describe his ideological position, Tutu described himself as a socialist.[462] In 1986, he related that "[a]ll my experiences with capitalism, I'm afraid, have indicated that it encourages some of the worst features in people. Eat or be eaten. It is underlined by the survival of the fittest. I can't buy that. I mean, maybe it's the awful face of capitalism, but I haven't seen the other face."[464] Also in the 1980s, he was reported as saying that "apartheid has given free enterprise a bad name".[465] While identifying with socialism, he opposed forms of socialism like Marxism–Leninism which promoted communism, being critical of Marxism–Leninism's promotion of atheism.[462] Tutu often used the aphorism that "African communism" is an oxymoron because—in his view—Africans are intrinsically spiritual and this conflicts with the atheistic nature of Marxism.[466] He was critical of the Marxist–Leninist governments in the Soviet Union and Eastern Bloc, comparing the way that they treated their populations with the way that the National Party treated South Africans.[439] In 1985, he stated that he hated Marxism–Leninism "with every fiber of my being" although sought to explain why black South Africans turned to it as an ally: "when you are in a dungeon and a hand is stretched out to free you, you do not ask for the pedigree of the hand owner."[467]

Nelson Mandela had foregrounded the idea of Ubuntu as being of importance to South Africa's political framework.[468] In 1986, Tutu had defined Ubuntu: "It refers to gentleness, to compassion, to hospitality, to openness to others, to vulnerability, to be available to others and to know that you are bound up with them in the bundle of life."[468] Reflecting this view of ubuntu, Tutu was fond of the Xhosa saying that "a person is a person through other persons".[411]

Theology

Tutu was attracted to Anglicanism because of what he saw as its tolerance and inclusiveness, its appeal to reason alongside scripture and tradition, and the freedom that its constituent churches had from any centralized authority.[340] Tutu's approach to Anglicanism has been characterised as having been Anglo-Catholic in nature.[469] He regarded the Anglican Communion as a family, replete with its internal squabbles.[470]

Tutu rejected the idea that any particular variant of theology was universally applicable, instead maintaining that all understandings of God had to be "contextual" in relating to the socio-cultural conditions in which they existed.[471] In the 1970s, Tutu became an advocate of both black theology and African theology, seeking ways to fuse the two schools of Christian theological thought.[472] Unlike other theologians, like John Mbiti, who saw the traditions as largely incompatible, Tutu emphasised the similarities between the two.[473] He believed that both theological approaches had arisen in contexts where black humanity had been defined in terms of white norms and values, in societies where "to be really human", the black man "had to see himself and to be seen as a chocolate coloured white man".[474] He also argued that both black and African theology shared a repudiation of the supremacy of Western values.[474] In doing so he spoke of an underlying unity of Africans and the African diaspora, stating that "All of us are bound to Mother Africa by invisible but tenacious bonds. She has nurtured the deepest things in us blacks."[473]

He became, according to Du Boulay, "one of the most eloquent and persuasive communicators" of black theology.[458] He expressed his views on theology largely through sermons and addresses rather than in extended academic treatises.[458] Tutu expressed the view that Western theology sought answers to questions that Africans were not asking.[475] For Tutu, two major questions were being posed by African Christianity; how to replace imported Christian expressions of faith with something authentically African, and how to liberate people from bondage.[476] He believed that there were many comparisons to be made between contemporary African understandings of God and those featured in the Old Testament.[113] He nevertheless criticised African theology for failing to sufficiently address contemporary societal problems, and suggested that to correct this it should learn from the black theology tradition.[474]

When chairing the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Tutu advocated an explicitly Christian model of reconciliation, as part of which he believed that South Africans had to face up to the damages that they had caused and accept the consequences of their actions.[477] As part of this, he believed that the perpetrators and beneficiaries of apartheid must admit to their actions but that the system's victims should respond generously, stating that it was a "gospel imperative" to forgive.[477] At the same time, he argued that those responsible had to display true repentance in the form of restitution.[477]

Reception and legacy

Gish noted that by the time of apartheid's fall, Tutu had attained "worldwide respect" for his "uncompromising stand for justice and reconciliation and his unmatched integrity".[478] According to Allen, Tutu "made a powerful and unique contribution to publicizing the antiapartheid struggle abroad", particularly in the United States.[479] In the latter country, he was able to rise to prominence as a South African anti-apartheid activist because—unlike Mandela and other members of the ANC—he had no links to the South African Communist Party and thus was more acceptable to Americans amid the Cold War anti-communist sentiment of the period.[480] In the United States, he was often compared to Martin Luther King Jr., with the African-American civil rights activist Jesse Jackson referring to him as "the Martin Luther King of South Africa".[481] After the end of apartheid, Tutu became "perhaps the world's most prominent religious leader advocating gay and lesbian rights", according to Allen.[339] Ultimately, Allen thought that perhaps Tutu's "greatest legacy" was the fact that he gave "to the world as it entered the twenty-first century an African model for expressing the nature of human community".[482]

During Tutu's rise to notability during the 1970s and 1980s, responses to him were "sharply polarized".[483] Noting that he was "simultaneously loved and hated, honoured and vilified",[484] Du Boulay attributed his divisive reception to the fact that "strong people evoke strong emotions".[485] Tutu gained much adulation from black journalists, inspired imprisoned anti-apartheid activists, and led to many black parents' naming their children after him.[483] For many black South Africans, he was a respected religious leader and a symbol of black achievement.[486] By 1984 he was—according to Gish—"the personification of the South African freedom struggle".[421] In 1988, Du Boulay described him as "a spokesman for his people, a voice for the voiceless".[400]

The response he received from South Africa's white minority was more mixed. Most of those who criticised him were conservative whites who did not want a shift away from apartheid and white-minority rule.[487] Many of these whites were angered that he was calling for economic sanctions against South Africa and that he was warning that racial violence was impending.[488] Said whites often accused him of being a tool of the communists.[462] This hostility was exacerbated by the government's campaign to discredit Tutu and distort his image,[489] which included repeatedly misquoting him to present his statements out of context.[490] According to Du Boulay, the SABC and much of the white press went to "extraordinary attempts to discredit him", something that "made it hard to know the man himself".[400] Allen noted that in 1984, Tutu was "the black leader white South Africans most loved to hate" and that this antipathy extended beyond supporters of the far-right government to liberals too.[183] The fact that he was "an object of hate" for many was something that deeply pained him.[485]

Hated by many white South Africans for being too radical, he was also scorned by many black militants for being too moderate.

— On Tutu in the mid-1980s, by Steven D. Gish, 2004[212]

Tutu also drew criticism from within the anti-apartheid movement and the black South African community. He was criticised repeatedly for making statements on behalf of black South Africans without consulting other community leaders first.[403] Some black anti-apartheid activists regarded him as too moderate,[491] and in particular too focused on cultivating white goodwill.[492] The African-American civil rights campaigner Bernice Powell, for instance, complained that he was "too nice to white people".[493] According to Gish, Tutu "faced the perpetual dilemma of all moderates – he was often viewed suspiciously by the two hostile sides he sought to bring together".[492] Tutu's critical view of Marxist-oriented communism and the governments of the Eastern Bloc, and the comparisons he drew between these administrations and far-right ideologies like Nazism and apartheid brought criticism from the South African Communist Party in 1984.[494] After the transition to universal suffrage, Tutu's criticism of presidents Mbeki and Zuma brought objections from their supporters; in 2006, Zuma's personal advisor Elias Khumalo claimed that it was a double standard that Tutu could "accept the apology from the apartheid government that committed unspeakable atrocities against millions of South Africans", yet "cannot find it in his heart to accept the apology" from Zuma.[495]

Honours

See also: List of honours of Desmond Tutu

Tutu gained many international awards and honorary degrees, particularly in South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States.[312] By 2003, he had approximately 100 honorary degrees;[496] he was, for example, the first person to be awarded an honorary doctorate by Ruhr University in West Germany, and the third person to whom Columbia University in the U.S. agreed to award an honorary doctorate off-campus.[497] Many schools and scholarships were named after him.[312] Mount Allison University in Sackville, New Brunswick was the first Canadian institution to award Tutu an honorary doctorate in 1988.[498] In 2000, the Munsieville Library in Klerksdorp was renamed the Desmond Tutu Library.[312] The Desmond Tutu School of Theology at Fort Hare University was launched in 2002.[312]

On 16 October 1984, Tutu was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The Nobel Committee cited his "role as a unifying leader figure in the campaign to resolve the problem of apartheid in South Africa".[499] This was seen as a gesture of support for him and the South African Council of Churches which he led at that time. In 1987 Tutu was awarded the Pacem in Terris Award,[500] named after a 1963 encyclical letter by Pope John XXIII that calls upon all people of good will to secure peace among all nations.[501]

In 1985 the City of Reggio Emilia named Tutu an honorary citizen together with Albertina Sisulu.[502]

In 2000, Tutu received the Common Wealth Award of Distinguished Service.[503]

In 2003, Tutu received the Golden Plate Award of the Academy of Achievement presented by Awards Council member Coretta Scott King.[504][505] In 2008, Governor Rod Blagojevich of Illinois proclaimed 13 May 'Desmond Tutu Day'.[506]

In 2010, he received the Lifetime African Achievement award from the Millennium Excellence Foundation based in Ghana,[507] a country he visited while sailing on a voyage of Semester at Sea.[508]

In 2015, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Tutu an Honorary Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour (CH).[509] The Queen appointed Tutu as a Bailiff Grand Cross of the Venerable Order of St. John in September 2017.[510]

In 2010, Tutu delivered the Bynum Tudor Lecture at the University of Oxford and became a visiting fellow at Kellogg College, Oxford.[511] In 2013, he received the £1.1m (US$1.6m) Templeton Prize for "his life-long work in advancing spiritual principles such as love and forgiveness".[512] In 2018 the fossil of a Devonian tetrapod was found in Grahamstown by Rob Gess of the Albany Museum; this tetrapod was named Tutusius umlambo in Tutu's honour.[513]

Writings

Tutu is the author of seven collections of sermons in addition to other writings:

  • Crying in the Wilderness, Eerdmans, 1982. ISBN 978-0-8028-0270-5[514]
  • Hope and Suffering: Sermons and Speeches, Skotaville, 1983. ISBN 978-0-620-06776-8[515]
  • The War Against Children: South Africa's Youngest Victims, Human Rights First, 1986. ISBN 9780934143004[516]
  • The Words of Desmond Tutu, Newmarket, 1989. ISBN 978-1-55704-719-9[517]
  • The Rainbow People of God: The Making of a Peaceful Revolution, Doubleday, 1994. ISBN 978-0-385-47546-4[518]
  • Worshipping Church in Africa, Duke University Press, 1995. ASIN B000K5WB02[519]
  • The Essential Desmond Tutu, David Phillips Publishers, 1997. ISBN 978-0-86486-346-1[520]
  • No Future Without Forgiveness, Doubleday, 1999. ISBN 978-0-385-49689-6[521]
  • An African Prayerbook, Doubleday, 2000. ISBN 978-0-385-47730-7[522]
  • God Has a Dream: A Vision of Hope for Our Time, Doubleday, 2004. ISBN 978-0-385-47784-0[523]
  • Desmond and the Very Mean Word, Candlewick, 2012. ISBN 978-0-763-65229-6[524]
  • The Book of Forgiving: The Fourfold Path for Healing Ourselves and Our World, HarperOne, 2015. ISBN 978-0062203571[525]
  • The Book of Joy: Lasting Happiness in a Changing World, coauthored by His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama, 2016, ISBN 978-0-67007-016-9

  301. ↑ Dershowitz, Alan (29 December 2021). "Bishop Tutu was the most influential anti-Semite of our time". JNS.org. Archived from the original on 7 September 2026. Retrieved 31 October 2024.
  302. ↑ Bernstein, David (1 January 2022). "The Late Bishop Desmond Tutu, Antisemite". Reason.com. Archived from the original on 8 September 2026. Retrieved 31 October 2024.
  303. ↑ Dadoo, Suraya (30 December 2021). "Desmond Tutu's inconvenient pro-Palestine legacy". The New Arab. Retrieved 31 October 2024. Almost as enduring as Tutu's support of the Palestinian liberation struggle has been smear campaigns against him, accusing the Archbishop of anti-Semitism. Tutu took on the pro-Israel lobby and the weaponisation of anti-Semitism head-on. Tutu wrote plainly: "…the Israeli government is placed on a pedestal and to criticise it is to be immediately dubbed anti-Semitic. People are scared in the US to say 'wrong is wrong' because the pro-Israeli lobby is powerful – very powerful. Well, so what?..." In doing so, Tutu angered the pro-Israel lobby in the US and in South Africa. In 2009, Alan Dershowitz referred to Tutu as 'a bigot and a racist'
  304. ↑ Rahman, Khaleda (28 December 2021). "Alan Dershowitz Calls Tutu 'Anti-Semite' and 'Bigot' After His Death". Newsweek. Retrieved 31 October 2024.
  305. ↑ Hanau, Shira (26 December 2021). "Desmond Tutu, anti-apartheid leader who identified with Jews and criticized Israel's treatment of Palestinians, dies at 90". Jewish Telegraphic Agency. Retrieved 31 October 2024. remarks that some Jewish leaders called antisemitic, earned Tutu criticism from some Jewish leaders. In his 1984 JTS speech, he addressed some of that criticism while further fanning its flames with references to a "Jewish lobby." "I was immediately accused of being antisemitic," Tutu said in his speech, referring to the reaction to an earlier speech. "I am sad because I think that it is a sensitivity in this instance that comes from an arrogance — the arrogance of power because Jews are a powerful lobby in this land and all kinds of people woo their support." In a 1989 visit to Israel and the West Bank, Tutu made the controversial suggestion during a visit to Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, that the Nazis ought to be forgiven for their crimes against the Jewish people.
